<reason>The motion as written prefers single-payer to employer systems "that tie access to work status," and A built its entire case on that text while B built its case on systems (Germany, Japan, Netherlands) that, by B's own admission in B4.1, untie access from work status. B never defended an access-tied system on its merits — only patches (COBRA, subsidies) that A plausibly framed as proving the defect — so B's route to victory required the judge to read the restrictive clause out of the motion, the kind of reframe the rules disfavor. A also fought B's fallback (one payer vs. many funds) to at least parity with the cherry-picking/risk-adjustment point and the deflation of fund-switching as "customer service, not clinical redundancy." B landed real hits — the B2.3 asymmetry charge (Canada ban as "policy choice" vs. COBRA as essence) went largely unanswered, the monopsony-queue mechanism was concrete, and B skillfully exploited A's private top-up concession — and B executed cleanly while A's Rebuttal 2 was clipped. But B's substantive wins could not repair the definitional problem, and A's closing crystallized it decisively: continuity is access, and nobody defended the tie.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Turn 3 concession trap ("That is not a rebuttal of the motion. That is the motion.") set the frame B never escaped; it was sealed by the Q1/A1 exchange where B conceded Germany unties continuity and A's closing equated continuity with access. B's strongest counter was the B2.3 one-standard asymmetry hit, which A never squarely answered.</best_rebuttal>
